power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: In decision-making, option values can arise from past experiences with rewards and punishments (experiential) or from explicit descriptions of outcomes and probabilities (descriptive).

While most studies have examined experiential and descriptive options separately, real-world decisions, such as deciding between a restaurant we visited before and one known through online reviews, often entail choosing between the two.
Recently, Garcia et al. (2023) revealed that experiential options are systematically neglected in such hybrid choices.
Yet, the cause of this experiential neglect remains unknown.

To test whether this phenomenon results from representational differences between experiential and descriptive options, we manipulated the learning architecture, test-phase feedback, stimulus format, and feedback format over five experiments (n = 375).
Participants showed reduced sensitivity to experiential losses relative to gains.
Importantly, experiential neglect persisted across all conditions, eliminating these hypotheses as explanations of this phenomenon.
Rather, we propose that neglect may stem from retrieval-based uncertainty in experiential valuation.
Together, these findings provide evidence for a cognitive constraint on the integration of experiential and described values in decision-making.
In everyday life, as in the laboratory, the subjective values that guide decision-making derive from two main sources of information: experience and description.
Experiential values are learned from past outcomes, whereas descriptive ones are informed by explicit information about decision-relevant variables, such as probabilities and rewards.

Real-world scenarios rarely involve only a single source of information (Hertwig et Erev 2009; Weiss-Cohen et al. 2016), as people routinely need to arbitrate between what they have learned from experience and what they know through external symbolic information.

text.text: Consider, for instance, choosing between a restaurant already visited in the past and one discovered through online reviews.
How experiential and descriptive values compete in such hybrid choices stands as a fundamental question.

However, most existing studies have examined experiential and descriptive decisions in isolation (Hertwig et Erev 2009; Hertwig et al. 2004; Barron et Erev 2003; Erev et al. 2017; Rakow et Newell 2010) which limits the possibility of testing this question in situations where subjective values are constructed in different ways.

text.text: A recent study by Garcia et al. (2023) addressed this issue by using an original hybrid decision-making paradigm in which participants chose between learned experiential options and explicitly described ones.

text.text: They found that individuals systematically underweight the options whose value is learned from experience -a phenomenon referred to as experiential value neglect.
Importantly, Garcia et al. (2023) ruled out alternative explanations for this neglect, including insufficient learning, lack of incentives, or extreme ambiguity aversion.

text.text: Yet, despite robust evidence for experiential value neglect, the mechanisms underlying the phenomenon remain poorly understood.
One possibility is that experiential neglect arises from representational differences between experiential and descriptive values.
According to this view, experiential and descriptive values may not be encoded in comparable representational spaces (Walasek et Brown 2024; Garcia et al. 2023).

text.text: Alternatively, experiential neglect may reflect constraints intrinsic to memory-based representations (Giguère et Love 2013).

ing accounts.
Specifically, the present study focuses on testing whether the phenomenon stems from representational asymmetries between experiential and descriptive values.

Among possible computational sources of representational differences, we examined whether experiential neglect arises from policy-based learning that prevents direct comparison with descriptive values (Bennett, Niv, et Langdon 2021; Hayden et Niv 2021); from distorted representations of descriptive option values (Prelec 1998; Kahneman et Tversky 1979; Tversky et Kahneman 1992); from the greater perceptual salience of symbolic representations (Bordalo, Gennaioli, et Shleifer 2013; Zilker et Pachur 2022a , 2022b , 2023; Krajbich, Armel, et Rangel 2010; Smith et Krajbich 2019); or from a representational incompatibility between experiential and descriptive values (Hertwig et Erev 2009; Stewart, Chater, et Brown 2006).

text.text: To address these questions, we independently manipulated key features of both the learning and the description components of the task.
Namely, we varied (i) the learning architecture, (ii) the test-phase feedback, (iii) the stimulus representation, and (iv) the feedback representation.
Across all manipulations, the value of experiential options, as inferred from choice patterns, exerted a reduced influence on choices between experiential and descriptive options.
Crucially, a declarative rating task (stated preferences) directly elicited the value of experiential options.
It confirmed that experiential values are correctly learned and can be accurately recovered.
This data further substantiates the idea of a genuine neglect of learned value information in hybrid choices.

Overall, we propose that experiential neglect stems from intrinsic features of memory-based representations, namely their perceived lower reliability relative to perceptually available options, rather than structural representational differences between options.
Finally, to further test the generalizability of the experiential neglect pattern, we adapted our analytical framework to assess the effect of the outcome valence dimension.

Indeed, both description-based and experience-based decision-making research shows important asymmetries in how values are constructed in the gain and loss domains (Kahneman et Tversky 1984; Palminteri et Pessiglione 2017; Palminteri et al. 2015).
text.formatted: Indeed, both description-based and experience-based decision-making research shows important asymmetries in how values are constructed in the gain and loss domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kahneman et Tversky 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Palminteri et Pessiglione 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Palminteri et al. 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore tested whether experiential value neglect generalized across this valence dimension, but also whether experiential values were learned and retrieved symmetrically in the gain and loss domains.

We found that experiential value neglect was present in each valence domain, and that negative experiential values were less accurately retrieved compared to positive ones -a result consistent with established asymmetric behavioral patterns across valence domains (Tversky et Kahneman 1992; Ruggeri et al. 2020; Yechiam et Hochman 2013; Palminteri et Lebreton 2022).

text.text: Together, these findings deepen our understanding of the cognitive constraints involved in integrating ex-periential and descriptive value information during decision-making.

text.text: Participants faced two types of options: experiential options (E-options) presented as eight abstract cues associated with different probability of winning points, and descriptive (or symbolic) options (S-options) symbolically depicting probabilities as pie-charts (Figure 1A).

text.text: As illustrated in Figure 1B, the experiment unfolded in four parts.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>, the experiment unfolded in four parts.

text.text: In the Learning (LE) phase, participants repeatedly chose between pairs of E-options and received information about both the obtained and the forgone outcome (complete feedback; +1/-1) on every trial, allowing them to learn the underlying gain probabilities associated with each cue.
Next, in the Test phase, participants made decisions without feedback, across 3 different modalities.
In the Experiential-Symbolic (ES) modality, previously learned E-options were paired with S-options, creating hybrid choice contexts.
In the Experiential-Experiential (EE) modality, choices were restricted to pairs of Eoptions.
Finally, the experiment concludes with the Stated Probability (SP) modality, in which participants directly reported the gain probability of each E-option on a continuous probabilistic scale.
Our main aim was to assess whether E-option values were systematically less influential in choice when competing against S-options.
To test this, we compared the subjective valuations of E-options inferred from the ES modality to those inferred in the EE and SP modalities.
For the choice-based modalities (ES and EE), we estimated the subjective value of each E-option from participants' choices.

Specifically, we examined how often a given E-option was chosen against alternatives of varying value (either S-options in ES or other E-options in EE), and fitted these choice rates with logistic functions (Figure 1C).
text.formatted: Specifically, we examined how often a given E-option was chosen against alternatives of varying value (either S-options in ES or other E-options in EE), and fitted these choice rates with logistic functions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: The midpoint (λ) of each fitted curve corresponds to the value of the alternative for which participants were equally likely to choose either option, that is, the indifference point.
This indifference point served as an estimate of the participant's subjective valuation of the E-option.
In the SP modality, subjective valuations were taken directly from participants' reported probabilities.
Because outcome magnitudes were fixed (+1/-1), differences in option value were entirely determined by gain probabilities.
For all modalities, we therefore examined how subjective values of the E-options scaled with their true underlying probabilities by extracting the slope of a linear fit across options (Figure 1D).
text.formatted: For all modalities, we therefore examined how subjective values of the E-options scaled with their true underlying probabilities by extracting the slope of a linear fit across options (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>).

text.text: The resulting slope indexes probability sensitivity, which reflects how strongly experiential information influences decisions.
Critically, smaller slope estimates in the ES modality relative to the EE modality indicate experien- tial neglect, that is, E-options are downweighted in hybrid choices.
We additionally compared ES slopes to those obtained in the SP modality to test for the same trend.
This analysis was conducted across five experiments in which we manipulated four key features of the learning and representational structure of options (Figure 1E).
text.formatted: This analysis was conducted across five experiments in which we manipulated four key features of the learning and representational structure of options (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1E</ref>).

text.text: Namely, we varied the learning architecture in Experiment 1, the test-phase feedback provided during hybrid choices in Experiment 2, the stimulus representation in Experiment 3, and the feedback representation in Experiment 4.
Previous research suggests that experiential options may be learned in a value-free, policy-based manner (Bennett et al. 2021; Hayden et Niv 2021).
text.formatted: Previous research suggests that experiential options may be learned in a value-free, policy-based manner <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bennett et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hayden et Niv 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In this case, choices are guided by a learned policy that selects the better option in a given context, without computing explicit intermediate values for each option (Vlaev et al. 2011).
text.formatted: In this case, choices are guided by a learned policy that selects the better option in a given context, without computing explicit intermediate values for each option <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Vlaev et al. 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, symbolic options provide optionspecific value representation that can be directly compared across contexts.
Because policy-based learning lacks these intermediate values, experiential options could be disadvantaged in hybrid choice, where individuals may rely on directly comparable symbolic values.
If experiential neglect were driven by this policybased learning, promoting option-specific learning of experiential values should reduce or eliminate this effect.
To test this, we manipulated the learning architecture in Experiment 1.

We compared a baseline learning phase (LE), in which participants trained on fixed pairs of E-options (likely to prompt a policy-based, contextual, learning strategy), with a manipulated LE in which participants trained on all possible pairwise combinations of E-options (referred to as the non-fixed pairs condition; less likely to promote a policy-based learning strategy).
Presenting all combinations prevents pairspecific learning policies, as each option must be evaluated across multiple relational contexts, promoting gen- eralized learning.
We verified that participants successfully learned to choose the best options, which was supported by choice accuracy being above chance levels (Figure S1 in Supplementary Materials).
text.formatted: We verified that participants successfully learned to choose the best options, which was supported by choice accuracy being above chance levels (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: We then estimated E-option subjective values from participants' choices in the ES and EE modalities using logistic indifference points (Figure 2A-B), and quantified how these values scaled with objective probabilities using linear regression slopes (Figure 2C).

text.text: We compared ES slopes with those from the EE and SP modalities to assess experiential neglect across conditions (Figure 2D).

text.text: To quantify experiential neglect, we applied Model M1, which compares ES and EE slope estimates across conditions using a linear mixed-effects framework (see Methods).

The modality effect, which gives slope difference between ES and EE within the fixed-pairs LE condition, was significantly negative (β = -0.257, SE = 0.036, z = -7.206, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.326, -0.187]), confirming the underweighting of E-options in hybrid choices within the baseline learning condition.

text.text: Critically, the ES-EE slope difference also remained significantly negative in the non-fixed pairs condition (β = -0.280, SE = 0.036, z = -7.872, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.350, -0.211]), confirming that experiential neglect persisted under nonfixed training, in which learning generalized across relational contexts.

text.text: Next, we examined the SP modality, which provides a direct elicitation of stated probabilities of E-option values that does not rely on an inference from choice behavior.
Because SP is performed at the end of the experiment, it also provides information about the retention and accessibility of learned experiential values.
We found that SP slopes were significantly higher than ES ones, despite the SP elicitation task occurring after the ES one (see Table S3A in Supplementary Materials).
text.formatted: We found that SP slopes were significantly higher than ES ones, despite the SP elicitation task occurring after the ES one (see Table <ref type="table">S3A</ref> in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: This suggests that experiential neglect emerges despite experiential values remaining accessible after ES choice.

Altogether, these results indicate that shifting from a learning environment that allows policy-learning to one that discourages pair-specific policies, favoring optionvalue learning, does not eliminate the underweighting of experiential options in hybrid decisions.
Another possibility is that experiential neglect reflects inaccurate or distorted subjective representations of option values.

Extensive literature shows that people distort probability distributions nonlinearly for both experiential and descriptive options, although differently (Prelec 1998; Kahneman et Tversky 1979), suggesting that subjective valuations may be imperfectly represented.

text.text: Critically, symbolic options are only introduced during the test phase, which prevents participants from refining their valuations beforehand.

This is particularly problematic as description-based choice probabilities are known to be distorted, with small probabilities being overestimated and large ones underestimated (Tversky et Kahneman 1992).
text.formatted: This is particularly problematic as description-based choice probabilities are known to be distorted, with small probabilities being overestimated and large ones underestimated <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Tversky et Kahneman 1992)</ref>.

text.text: This could create asymmetries between experiential and symbolic options in hybrid choices, thereby contributing to experiential neglect.
To test this account, Experiment 2 introduced outcome feedback during the test phase to attenuate potential representational distortion.

We contrasted our original baseline condition ('without feedback') with a condition in which participants received outcome feedback (+1 or -1) after each decision in both ES and EE modalities (feedback condition).

Crucially, this outcome feedback was complete (i.e. provided for both chosen and unchosen options) and provided for both E-and S-options, allowing not only further updating of experiential values but also correction of putatively distorted subjective representations of symbolic probabilities.
If experiential neglect were driven by biased valuation of symbolic options, providing corrective feedback should reduce or eliminate the asymmetry.
As in Experiment 1, participants in both conditions demonstrated successful learning during the initial phase, with choice accuracy exceeding chance levels (Figure S1 in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: These findings suggest that experiential neglect is not explained by distortions that test-phase feedback could correct.
A further hypothesis is that symbolic options may dominate choice simply because they are more salient.

Symbolic options explicitly convey probability distributions in a visually clear and aesthetically appealing format, which may preferentially capture attention and shape the allocation of cognitive resources during decisionmaking (Yantis et Egeth 1999; Desimone et Duncan 1995; Treisman et Gelade 1980).

text.text: Contemporary models of choice, including attentional drift-diffusion and related evidence-accumulation frameworks, posit that attention dynamically modulates the weight of information in value construction, such that attended options exert a disproportionate influence on evidence accumulation and choice (Krajbich et al. 2010; Smith et Krajbich 2019; Zilker et Pachur 2022a , 2022b , 2023).

text.text: Under this view, symbolic representations may bias the decision process by receiving greater attentional weighting, thereby amplifying their contribution to the decision variable, while experiential information exerts a weaker influence.
In Experiment 3, we therefore changed the visual representation of S-option lotteries to reduce their visual complexity (and consequently their saliency).

We tested two new representation conditions: one where explicit probability information was removed from the original colored pie-charts (called pie-charts), and another where S-options were presented as textual descriptions of probabilities without visual cues (denoted numerical).

These manipulations are intended to reduce, respectively, the encoding precision and attentional salience of the probabilistic information of S-options, which in turn should increase the weight of experiential options in choice.
As in previous experiments, participants correctly learned E-option values (Figure S1 in Supplementary Materials).

Finally, experiential and symbolic options differ not only in how their values are acquired (learned vs described), but also in the very nature of the representation through which those values are encoded.
Experiential options are learned through sequences of trial-bytrial individual outcomes, from which participants can internally construct an average or probability estimate (Stewart et al. 2006).
text.formatted: Experiential options are learned through sequences of trial-bytrial individual outcomes, from which participants can internally construct an average or probability estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Stewart et al. 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, symbolic options are represented as explicit lotteries, directly encoding full probability distributions in a structured format.

Such representational asymmetry has been suggested as a partial explanation of the description-experience gap (Hertwig et Erev 2009) and may create a format incompatibility at decision time when the two kinds of options are compared directly.
text.formatted: Such representational asymmetry has been suggested as a partial explanation of the description-experience gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hertwig et Erev 2009)</ref> and may create a format incompatibility at decision time when the two kinds of options are compared directly.

text.text: In hybrid choices, experiential values may need to be translated from an internally constructed summary into a lottery-like format in order to be compared with symbolic options.
This translation process may impose a cognitive cost rendering experiential information less accessible, and thereby reducing its influence on choice, which we tested in experiments 4A and 4B.

We compared our baseline condition in which trial-level E-option outcomes were presented as numerical values (reward condition), with a new condition in which E-outcomes were instead displayed as pie charts (lottery condition, Soukupova, Garcia, et Palminteri 2026).
The lottery condition aligns the representational format of experiential feedback with the S-option lottery format, which allows the two options to be encoded using a shared representation.
Note that the lottery condition doesn't remove the learning component as participants still need to associate these probabilities to abstract cues.
If experiential neglect arises from a translation cost, this manipulation should reduce or eliminate its effect.

To test this across different learning architectures (see Experiment 1), we designed an Experiment 4A which implements fixed pairs during the learning phase, and an Experiment 4B which implements non-fixed pairs.
Once again, participants correctly learned E-option values in the LE phase, and to a same degree in experiments 4A and 4B (Figure S1 in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: Across our five experiments, we reported highly consistent patterns of evidence supporting experiential neglect.
To further check the robustness of the phenomenon beyond single experiment-level, we performed random-effects meta-analyses on conditionlevel estimates (see Methods).

The meta-analytical estimate of the difference between ES and EE scaling slopes confirms a highly robust and consistent negative effect across experiments (Figure 4, left; β = -0.239, SE = 0.016, z = -5.326 p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.275, -0.204]).

text.text: Beyond demonstrating the robustness of this phenomenon, the central focus of our study is to understand what causes experiential neglect.
One possibility was that it arises due to representational differences between experiential and descriptive values.
To address this, we systematically tested four major classes of explanations across five experiments.

Our findings suggest that experiential neglect is not explained by policybased learning (Experiment 1), distorted valuation of symbolic options (Experiment 2), the greater perceptual salience of symbolic options (Experiment 3) or incompatible outcome formats between experiential and symbolic options (Experiment 4A and 4B).
With these alternatives unable to account for neglect, we suggest that experiential neglect arises from another intrinsic property of experiential options.
One remaining distinguishing feature is that experiential values must be retrieved from memory at the time of choice, whereas symbolic option values are immediately available.
As retrieval from memory is a limited process that can constrain decision making (Giguère et Love 2013), experiential neglect might arise at that stage.
text.formatted: As retrieval from memory is a limited process that can constrain decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Giguère et Love 2013)</ref>, experiential neglect might arise at that stage.

text.text: A first possibility is that experiential neglect reflects a retrieval cost: participants may disregard experiential options because retrieving their values incurs a cognitive cost (Bordalo et al. 2020; Dukas 1999), making explicitly described symbolic options more attractive to rely on.
text.formatted: A first possibility is that experiential neglect reflects a retrieval cost: participants may disregard experiential options because retrieving their values incurs a cognitive cost <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bordalo et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dukas 1999)</ref>, making explicitly described symbolic options more attractive to rely on.

text.text: This account predicts that experiential neglect should primarily arise when retrieval itself can be avoided, like in hybrid choices.
However, the ES and EE trials were interleaved, with their order randomized while holding the experiential option constant.

Thus, the value of an experiential option could be retrieved during the EE choices (as suggested by high accuracy in those trials) and maintained in working memory for the subsequent ES choices with no additional retrieval cost.
Yet experiential neglect still emerges, suggesting that avoidance of retrieval per se is unlikely to be the sole driver of the effect.
We instead propose that experiential neglect arises from subjective uncertainty associated with the retrieval of experiential values.
Crucially, this uncertainty does not imply that the value is incompletely learned or in-accurately stored.
Rather, even when experiential values are correctly learned, they may be associated with reduced confidence at retrieval.
Participants may therefore discount experiential information because they are less confident in the reliability or precision of retrieved value estimates.

In hybrid decision-making contexts, such uncertainty can lead to a down-weighting of experiential information (Lee et Hare 2023), especially when it competes with symbolic options whose attributes are explicitly displayed and therefore perceived as more certain.

text.text: Importantly, this does not imply that symbolic valuation is objectively noise-free.
Constructing symbolic values can also involve substantial cognitive uncertainty and computational noise (Woodford 2012; Enke et Graeber 2023; Oprea 2024).
text.formatted: Constructing symbolic values can also involve substantial cognitive uncertainty and computational noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Woodford 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Enke et Graeber 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Oprea 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the immediate external availability of symbolic attributes may nevertheless increase subjective confidence in their reliability relative to experiential options, even if both formats are objectively noisy.
Several aspects of our results help characterize the role of retrieval-based uncertainty in experiential value neglect.
First, experiential value neglect does not stem from poor memory quality or noisy value representations.
If it did, participants should perform poorly when relying solely on experiential values.
Instead, experiential options are evaluated relatively accurately in EE and SP modalities.

Second, because experiential values may be associated with subjective uncertainty at retrieval and thus be treated as ambiguous, participants may be ambiguity averse and avoid them (Fox et Tversky 1995).
text.formatted: Second, because experiential values may be associated with subjective uncertainty at retrieval and thus be treated as ambiguous, participants may be ambiguity averse and avoid them <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fox et Tversky 1995)</ref>.

text.text: However, experiential neglect cannot be reduced to a general aversion to ambiguity.
Our results do not indicate that experiential options are chosen less overall as they would if participants were ambiguity averse.

Rather, their values are less influential in hybrid choices, leading to decisions that are suboptimal given the experiential value: overselection of experiential options when the symbolic option has a negative expected value, and underselection when it has a positive expected value.
We therefore propose that experiential neglect reflects underconfidence in experiential value estimates rather than imprecision or ambiguity per se.
In our task, it is difficult to fully dissociate underconfidence arising during learning from underconfidence arising during retrieval.

Based on the interpretations developed above, we propose that experiential neglect is a pervasive feature of hybrid choices in which experiential values must be retrieved from memory at the time of decision.
Under this view, neglect should emerge specifically when experiential options compete with symbolic options whose values are immediately available.
Empirical investigations of such hybrid choice settings remain relatively scarce.
One notable exception is a recent study by Tiede, Gaissmaier, et Pachur (2025), which did not report systematic neglect of experiential values in hybrid choices.
text.formatted: One notable exception is a recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Tiede, Gaissmaier, et Pachur (2025)</ref>, which did not report systematic neglect of experiential values in hybrid choices.

text.text: At first glance, this result may appear to con-flict with our findings.
However, a closer examination of their experimental design reveals an important methodological difference in how experiential values are constructed.
In their task, participants choose between a symbolic option and an experiential option whose value is learned within the same trial through outcome sampling.
Specifically, before making their choice, participants can freely sample outcomes from the experiential option as many times as they wish, directly observing its payoff distribution.
Only after this free sampling phase do they decide between the experiential and the symbolic option.
As a result, experiential values are acquired and can be immediately used for choice, substantially minimizing the uncertainty associated with memory retrieval.
The contrast between their findings and ours does not contradict the existence of experiential neglect, and it is consistent with retrieval-based uncertainty contributing to it.
Having demonstrated the robustness of experiential neglect in this lab experiment, a crucial question remains of whether this phenomenon generalizes in real world scenarios.
In our controlled experimental design, participants can trust the objective and reliable nature of the descriptive information.
However, in real-life settings, descriptive information is rarely as precise or controlled (Hertwig et Erev 2009).
text.formatted: However, in real-life settings, descriptive information is rarely as precise or controlled <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hertwig et Erev 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Some descriptive information like real-life gambling lotteries or medication side-effects statistics mirror our experiment's controlled information, but others introduce social and contextual uncertainty.
For example, restaurant ratings rely on others' subjective experiences, and technical metrics such as nutrition scores are often based on expert assessments.
If experiential neglect is driven by a general aversion to perceived unreliable information, will the opposite pattern emerge in naturalistic contexts including other sources of uncertainty?
Will the distrust of socially derived descriptive information outweigh retrieval-based uncertainty for experiential information?
Future work should assess whether experiential neglect persists in more ecological settings where descriptive information has some level of social construction (e.g.
"The previous 500 participants reported that this lottery has an 80% chance of giving a point and a 20% chance of losing a point.").

text.text: However, the persistence of experiential value neglect does not necessarily imply that experiential and symbolic values lack a common representational format.

Rather, it suggests that values originating from different informational systems may enter the decision process with different levels of subjective reliability, accessibility, or computational priority.
The core issue, then, is not whether values can be compared, but how the decision system integrates heterogeneous value representations under cognitive and computational constraints.

Attentional allocation (Roe, Busemeyer, et Townsend 2001; Busemeyer et al. 2019), uncertainty (Daw, Niv, et Dayan 2005; Lee, Shimojo, et O'Doherty 2014), and resource demands (Kool, Gershman, et Cushman 2017; Shenhav, Botvinick, et Cohen 2013) may trigger heuristic or priority-based mechanisms rather than fully symmetric integration.

text.text: Under this interpretation, a shared representational scale may be sufficient for within-format comparison while remaining insufficient to guarantee symmetric integration across heterogeneous informational systems.

The present findings therefore suggest that hybrid choices involve not only option-level valuation, but also meta-level arbitration (Sripada 2026; Lieder et al. 2018) among systems differing in retrieval demands, subjective reliability, and computational accessibility.

text.text: In such frameworks, decision-making may not only depend on the estimated value of available options, but also on the inferred reliability of the systems generating those values.

In this sense, experiential and descriptive information may be encoded in partially comparable formats, while their influence on choice remains asymmetrically weighted according to the accessibility and subjective reliability of the underlying representations at the time of decision.
In addition to our general experiential value neglect findings, our results also reveal two distinct but complementary effects of valence on experiential valuation.
First, experiential neglect was observed in both gain and loss domains.

Although this effect was more robust at the meta-analytic level than when examined separately within individual experimental conditions, its presence across domains indicates that experiential neglect is not specific to either gains or losses.
Instead, the tendency to underweight experiential values in hybrid choices appears to be a general feature of experiential decisionmaking, seemingly independent of outcome valence.
Second, we observed a systematic asymmetry between gain and loss domains.
Across all modalities, experiential information associated on average with losses was systematically less influential than equivalent gainrelated information.

At first glance, this finding appears to run counter to the intuition behind Prospect Theory, which posits that "losses loom larger than gains" and are therefore weighted more strongly in decision-making (Kahneman et Tversky 1984 , 1979).
text.formatted: At first glance, this finding appears to run counter to the intuition behind Prospect Theory, which posits that "losses loom larger than gains" and are therefore weighted more strongly in decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kahneman et Tversky 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is important to note that loss aversion primarily concerns asymmetries in the subjective magnitude of outcomes, rather than sensitivity to probability information.
In our task, outcome magnitudes were fixed (+1 or -1) such that only probabilities varied.
The observed effect therefore can be better conceptualized as a form of loss probability underweighting, rather than reduced aversion to losses per se.

This asymmetry aligns with broader evidence for a positivity bias in learning and decision-making (Palminteri et Lebreton 2022; Sharot et Garrett 2016; Eil et Rao 2011), whereby positive information is integrated more efficiently than negative information.
text.formatted: This asymmetry aligns with broader evidence for a positivity bias in learning and decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Palminteri et Lebreton 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Sharot et Garrett 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Eil et Rao 2011)</ref>, whereby positive information is integrated more efficiently than negative information.

text.text: Nonetheless, an important limitation of our design is that gains and losses were manipulated only through their probabilities, not their magnitudes.

As a result, we cannot determine whether the observed loss underweighting arises from distortions in probability weighting, differences in subjective outcome valuation, or an interaction between the two.
Disentangling these mechanisms will require future work that independently manipulates both outcome magnitudes and probabilities across valence domains.

text.text: Across all experiments, participants encountered two types of options: experiential options (E-options) represented as eight abstract cues with probabilistic outcomes or symbolic options (S-options) presented as eleven pie charts explicitly depicting gain probabilities.
The gain probabilities associated with Eoptions were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 whilst the S-options additionally had 0, 0.5 and 1.
The additional symbolic probabilities were included to fully span the probability space and facilitate estimation of choice functions.
In both types of options, displayed in Figure 1A, gains (+1 point) and losses (-1 point) occur according to these associated probabilities.

text.text: As shown in Figure 1B, the first phase, named Learning (LE) phase, presented participants with pairs of E-options.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>, the first phase, named Learning (LE) phase, presented participants with pairs of E-options.

text.text: On each trial, participants selected one Eoption and received complete feedback (+1 or -1) allowing them to gradually infer the underlying probability value attached.
All possible pairwise combinations of options were presented twice, resulting in a total of 112 trials.
The presentation order followed a structured block design: within each block, one E-option is held constant while the second E-option varies.
Once all combinations within a block were shown, the task proceeded to the next block, where a different option is held constant.
This block structure ensured repeated exposure while preserving randomized presentation and minimizing sequential dependencies.
The order of blocks and the order of trials within each block were randomized, furthermore, the left/right display of options were also randomized.
Following learning, participants completed a test phase without feedback, comprising three modalities.
In the Experiential-Symbolic (ES) modality, participants chose between E-options learned in the LE phase and S-options, creating hybrid decision contexts.
In the Experiential-Experiential (EE) modality, choices were restricted to pairs of E-options.
All possible pairwise combinations were presented only once.
ES and EE trials were interleaved within the same block structure, with one E-option held constant per block while the other varied across trials.
Block order, trial order, and left/right positioning were randomized.
In total, participants completed 88 ES trials and 56 EE trials.
Finally, the experiment concluded with the Stated Probability (SP) modality, which employed a different elicitation method.
In this modality, participants were asked to estimate the gain probability associated with each E-option by answering the question: "What are the odds this symbol gives a +1?".
Responses were provided using a continuous slider ranging from 0% to 100% in 5% increments.
The initial position of the slider was randomized across trials (discretely among 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, and 70) to reduce anchoring effects.

Due to changes in the Prolific participant pool over this time span, we implemented two inclusion criteria, which were not present in the 2022 experiments, to ensure demographic consistency across experimental sets.
Specifically, for the 2025 experiments, only participants aged between 18 and 40 were eligible and gender quotas were applied to maintain a 1:1 ratio of male and female participants.
More generally, subjects that participated in one study were not eligible for the other experiments.
In addition to a fixed participation fee (mean £5.42 across experiments), participants' choices were incentivized with a performance-based bonus of up to £6.76.
On average across experiments, participants received a bonus of £5.27.
The study was approved by the INSERM (Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale) Ethics Committee (IRB00003888).
All participants gave informed consent and were briefed on the incentivization procedure prior to starting the experiment.
To ensure data quality, catch-trials during the ES/EE test phase were included.
In those trials, two S-options were presented, one clearly superior in terms of expected value.
Participants who failed any of these catch trials were excluded from analysis.

text.text: To check for experiential neglect, we compared the subjective value of E-options in the ES modality to the one in EE modality.
We additionally compared the ES E-option valuation to the one from the SP modality.
We first inferred the subjective value of the different E-options.
To do so, we studied the probability of choosing a specific E-option over an S-option (for ES modality) or over another E-option (for EE modality).
As portrayed in Figure 1C, we fitted logistic functions (see Equation 1) to the choice rate regarding that E-option for each participant.
text.formatted: As portrayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>, we fitted logistic functions (see Equation <ref type="formula">1</ref>) to the choice rate regarding that E-option for each participant.

text.text: Equation 1: -λ)  The logistic function included two free parameters: the sensitivity β parameter and the λ midpoint.

These parameters were estimated individually for each participant using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) estimation by minimizing the negative logposterior probability using the L-BFGS-B algorithm.
This was done with Python's (v3.12.15) minimize function (method: "L-BFGS-B", maximum iterations: 10,000), from scipy.optimize module (scipy v1.18.1).
Initial parameter values were set to 1 (β) and 0.5 (λ), with constraints of β ∈ [0.01, 30] and λ ∈ (0, 1).
We also tested maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation with a weak Gamma prior on β (shape α = 2, scale θ = 3), but this did not substantially improve parameter recovery.
Thus, we retained the MLE approach.
Parameter recovery results for both methods are provided in Supplementary Materials (Figures S13) and fitting scripts can be found on https://github.com/caropio/RandC_Followup_Analysis.
text.formatted: Parameter recovery results for both methods are provided in Supplementary Materials (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S13</ref>) and fitting scripts can be found on <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/caropio/RandC_Followup_Analysis">https://github.com/caropio/RandC_Followup_Analysis</ref>.

text.text: The fitted midpoint of the logistic curve served as the indifference point of that E-option, the point at which a participant is equally likely to choose the E-option or its alternative.
This midpoint thus reflects the subjective valuation of that E-option for that specific participant.
We estimated these indifference points for all E-options in both the ES and EE modalities.
For the SP modality, the subjective values are taken directly from the participants' stated probabilities.
We then examined the inferred subjective values of E-options as a function of their objective underlying probabilities.
We fitted a linear function across E-options and extracted the slope (see Figure 1D).
text.formatted: We fitted a linear function across E-options and extracted the slope (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>).

text.text: This slope provides a measure of probability sensitivity, indexing the degree to which differences in objective probabilities are translated into differences in subjective value.
Because subjective values are inferred from choice behavior, the slope serves as an indirect behavioral proxy for the effective weighting of experiential probability information in decision-making.
Under standard revealed-preference assumptions (McFadden 1974; Train 2003), the more weight a variable carries in option values, the more choices change as the variable changes.
text.formatted: Under standard revealed-preference assumptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(McFadden 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Train 2003)</ref>, the more weight a variable carries in option values, the more choices change as the variable changes.

text.text: Thus, information that plays a larger role in choice should give rise to systematic choice differences as it varies.

Accordingly, a slope close to zero indicates low probability sensitivity, such that differences in experiential probabilities carry little informative value for choice, reflecting weak weighting of experiential information.
Conversely, a slope close to one indicates that experiential probability information is translated into highly sensitive subjective valuation which in turn can meaningfully inform choice.
Crucially, we compared the slope estimates of the ES and EE modalities within each participant to test whether the same experiential information is used differently depending on context.

A smaller slope estimate in the ES modality relative to the EE one indicates experiential neglect, reflecting a reduced weighting of experiential values in choices where they compete with symbolic options.
We additionally compared ES slopes to those obtained in the SP modality to test for the same pattern.
All statistical analyses used an alpha level of 0.05 for statistical tests and were conducted using Python v3.12.15.
Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were fitted using the mixedlm function from the statsmodels.formula.api module (statsmodels v0.15.0).
Fixed-effect significance was assessed using z-statistics (approximate Wald tests).

When testing effects were not directly estimated by the model, linear contrasts were constructed by specifying contrast vectors over the fixed-effect coefficients (including main effects and interaction terms) and evaluated using the model's .t_test() method, which computes Wald tests of linear hypotheses over the fixed-effect coefficients.
To derive meta-analytical estimates, we conducted random-effects meta-analyses using experimentand condition-level regression results (estimate and variance).
Random-effects models were chosen to account for expected heterogeneity across experiments and conditions.
Between-experiment variance was estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).
Meta-analyses were implemented using the meta_regression() function (method = "reml") of the pymare package (v0.0.13).
Some statistical results reported in figures were obtained using paired t-tests, with data grouped either by participant or by experimental condition, depending on the analysis.
These tests were performed using the ttest_rel function from the scipy.stats module (scipy v1.18.1).

All statistical results are reported using: estimates (β), standard errors (SE), z-statistics (z) for LMMs and metaanalytic aggregations, Student's t-statistics t and degrees of freedom df (t(df)) for paired comparisons, p-values (p), 95% confidence intervals (CI).

The model is a Linear Mixed Model of data from the ES and EE modalities.
The dependent variable is the slope estimate.
The fixed effects are the following: Condition (categorical: session0 [reference], session1 -see specifications per experiment), Modality (categorical: EE [reference], ES) and interaction.
The model includes random intercepts for participants.

The Modality coefficient β2 captures the slope difference between ES and EE within the session0 condition.
The interaction term captures whether the ES-EE slope difference is larger or smaller in the session1 condition compared to the session0 one.
The sum of the modality and interaction coefficients captures the slope difference between ES and EE within the session1 condition (which was tested using constructed linear contrasts).

The model is a Linear Mixed Model of data from the EE, ES or SP modality.
The dependent variable is the slope estimate.
The fixed effects are the following: Condition (categorical: session0 [reference], session1 -see specifications per experiment), Valence (categorical: Gain [reference], Loss) and interaction.
The model includes random intercepts for participants.
Random slopes were not included because models including them frequently failed to converge.
The model is estimated separately for ES, EE and SP modalities.

The Valence coefficient β2 captures the difference in slope estimates between the loss and gain domains within the session0 condition, indicating the relative probability sensitivity for losses compared with gains, in that condition.
The interaction term captures whether the loss-gain slope difference is larger or smaller in the session1 condition compared to the ses-sion0 one.

The sum of the valence and interaction coefficients captures the slope difference between loss and gain within the session1 condition (which was tested using constructed linear contrasts), and thus a negative co-efficient would indicate lower probability sensitivity for losses compared with gains in that condition.
